instruction: Create a single-page SVG showcase of an Indian auto rickshaw (tuk-tuk). Make the vehicle the dominant focal object and visibly include its three-wheel structure, enclosed passenger cabin, driver windshield, canopy roof, headlamp, mirrors, handlebars, mudguards, and small ornamental details. Use convincing three-quarter perspective, layered shading, and a lively street-inspired palette. Put strong emphasis on a coherent composition, precise vector craft, dimensionality, and polished finish.

history.critique: Brief & Intent: nearly all required parts are present, but the three-wheel logic is broken — two wheels are clustered at the front under the headlamp and only one sits at the rear, so the vehicle reads as two-front-wheel instead of one-front/two-rear, undermining both the 'three-wheel structure' requirement and the three-quarter perspective. Handlebars and mirrors are reduced to a single dot each, so 'visibly include' is only marginally met; the headlamp is a red donut that reads as a taillight. Copy errors ('One canopy, one canopy of colour'; the Devanagari 'शारत' is not टुकटुक) undercut the field-study intent. Clarity & Hierarchy: the oversized serif title out-competes the vehicle for first focal priority; the 12 on-canvas labels are tiny, several sit directly on the body, and leader lines cross each other and the artwork; the anatomy list is truncated in the viewport (09–12 not visible), breaking the numbering contract at first glance. Visual System & Craft: shading is mostly flat two-tone, contradicting the 'layered shading / dimensionality' claim and the 'shaded by hand' copy; other craft gaps include hard edges, a cartoonish headlamp, marquee bulbs floating above the roof with no mounting, and a flat dark side window that reads as a hole. The dotted stage and serif/sans/mono type system are coherent and genuinely good. Expressiveness: the annotated field-study concept is distinctive, but the vehicle's muted teal palette feels more product-render than 'lively street-inspired'; the striped awning and marquee dots are the only truly characterful moments. Real trade-offs: the annotation layer adds educational value but directly dilutes the 'dominant focal object' and 'polished finish' goals; the dark stage makes the vehicle pop but suppresses the requested street-lively palette; keeping all 12 labels on-canvas fights the clean-finish goal.
history.suggestion: One prioritized plan (all inline SVG/CSS, no external assets): 1) Rebuild wheel/ground geometry first — one front wheel centered under the headlamp and front fender, a near rear wheel under the cabin tail, and a far rear wheel offset up-left, partially occluded by the body and darkened one value; align all contact points to a single ground line with one soft elliptical contact shadow. 2) Make the small required parts actually visible: a T-shaped handlebar with grips and steering stem in front of the driver, two mirror stalks (near + far), a larger framed windshield with a wiper, an amber/white headlamp with a lens highlight, a visible exhaust stub, and a rear mudguard arc. 3) Add layered shading via inline SVG gradients plus 2–3 value overlay paths per panel (top light, mid, core shadow) and a warm rim light on roof/canopy edges, keeping the flat-vector language but with real value steps. 4) Rebalance composition: scale the vehicle up ~15–20% and center it in the stage; convert on-canvas text labels to small numbered dots only, revealing the text label on hover (matching the existing 'hover to isolate' list), and route any remaining leaders so they never cross the body; show all 12 anatomy rows (two columns or internal scroll) so nothing is truncated. 5) Push the palette street-lively: saturate the teal or add a secondary yellow/red panel and trim, keep the orange-cream canopy, and add 2–3 small ornaments (tassel, side stripe, 'for hire' sign) without adding new required parts. 6) Fix copy: remove the 'one canopy, one canopy' repetition and correct the Devanagari to टुकटुक. 7) Let the vehicle lead: slightly reduce the title scale or raise the stage so the rickshaw, not the wordmark, is the first focal point.
